records.name: Chiapas
records.current_summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, but Chiapas is one of ten of Mexico's 32 states whose legislatures had still created no legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, despite supreme-court doctrine establishing the right. The practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico, since document mismatch triggers questioning at checkpoints, banks and clinics — with no local administrative cure; courts can order recognition case by case.

Rights reporting on a neighbouring non-reforming state (an unsolved killing of a trans activist, health staff outting patients, no hate-motivation provisions) illustrates the institutional climate such refusal sustains, though no Chiapas-specific violence series is documented in the surviving sources. Mexico City's 2024 transfemicide law marks the reform benchmark this state has not followed.
records.current_localsOnly: The absence of a legal gender recognition procedure bites hardest on residents' documents and registry dealings; visitors use home documents and never apply locally.
records.current_outOfScope: General cartel violence, kidnapping and theft drive foreign travel advisories for parts of Mexico and affect all travellers equally; they do not move trans-specific risk here.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Chiapas has NOT reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025, leaving trans residents with mismatched documents and case-by-case judicial recourse only.

HRW (6 Mar 2024) report: in Tabasco, murders and violence against trans people have shaken the community; the state has no legal gender recognition procedure, so trans people face document-mismatch discrimination in employment, health, education and financial transactions - hospital staff called out interviewees' legal names in waiting rooms. HRW urges a simple self-identification procedure. Retained for Chiapas as the neighbouring non-reforming state's documented climate (unsolved killing of a trans activist, no hate-motivation provisions).

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

records.name: Chihuahua
records.current_summary:
Chihuahua has functioning gender-recognition machinery without a state statute: after the state civil code still required a judicial process, a 2019 supreme-court ruling struck that requirement down, and the civil registry now performs administrative recognitions. The state legislature itself had enacted no recognition law as of March 2025. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile state ordinance is documented in the surviving sources.

The surviving audited sources for this record document no state-specific incident series; the national backdrop for trans people remains violent and impunity-prone, with the capital's 2024 transfemicide law the reform benchmark other states are measured against.
records.current_localsOnly: Recognition here runs through a court-forced registry procedure rather than a statute - a resident documents question that does not touch visitors.
records.current_outOfScope: General cartel violence, kidnapping and theft drive foreign travel advisories for parts of Mexico and affect all travellers equally; they do not move trans-specific risk here.

sources.claim: HRW (31 Mar 2025) Trans Rights in Mexico, state-by-state table: 22 of Mexico's 32 states now have an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure. Chihuahua has enacted no legislative recognition reform as of March 2025, but its Civil Registry maintains an administrative practice following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling that struck down the judicial-process requirement.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City's congress passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years - the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, galvanised by the 2016 murder of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro; the law obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

records.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
records.current_summary: No criminalisation of trans presence. In 2018 the state congress passed a Civil Registry law establishing an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity - among the earlier such enactments in Mexico - and no region-specific incident or enforcement pattern was found; visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2018 registry-law gender-identity procedure is resident-facing civil-registry machinery.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025), covering which of the 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure and the Supreme Court rulings that drove expansion. For Coahuila: the 2018 Law on the Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila (arts. 124-128) established an administrative procedure for recognition of self-identified gender identity.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a non-reforming state behaves.

Guardian report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (the 'Paola Buenrostro law', approved 18 July 2024), in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table states that in 2018 Coahuila's congress passed a law creating the Law on Civil Registry of the State of Coahuila, establishing an administrative procedure for the recognition of self-identified gender identity, and links the official gazette text of the reform (arts. 124-128, pp. 20-21). This is the jurisdiction-specific legal fact (law, year, administrative-procedure mechanism) that the record's summary asserts.

sources.title: Permitirán nueva identidad legal por cambio de género - El Heraldo de Saltillo
sources.claim: El Heraldo de Saltillo reports (13 November 2018) that proposals from several parliamentary groups and an initiative by former governor Rubén Moreira shaped the new Ley del Registro Civil del Estado presented to the plenary of the Coahuila congress, which proposes the legal recognition of trans people under their new legal personality; the dictamen, approved by unanimity, reforms article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza and creates the Civil Registry law, whose article 2, fraction XI, defines gender identity as the personal and internal conviction. This is a dated, outcome-specific local-news account of the 2018 law the record cites as 'among the earlier such enactments in Mexico'.

sources.title: En Coahuila, alrededor de mil 500 personas han formalizado su cambio de identidad de género - El Heraldo de Saltillo
sources.claim: El Heraldo de Saltillo reports (31 March 2023) that Coahuila's Civil Registry director, Ricardo Malacara, said that from early 2019 to March 2023 around 1,500 people in Coahuila had completed the legal gender-identity change procedure before the Civil Registry, in both directions (male to female and female to male), and that approximately 3,500 transgender citizens held formal jobs at companies operating in the state. This is the only region-specific implementation-outcome data found for Coahuila and shows the administrative procedure the record describes is functioning at scale.

records.name: Colima
records.current_summary:
Colima is governed by Mexico's federal framework: same-sex conduct is not criminalised, legal gender recognition remains an unresolved state-by-state mosaic that courts have pressed legislatures to complete, and the country overall is one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people with high impunity, as the capital's 2024 transfemicide law reflects.

The audited record documents no Colima-specific law, procedure, ordinance or incident series.

sources.claim: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years — the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, after Nayarit (up to 60 years). In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, with transfemicide impunity thought higher still. For this record: benchmarks the national lethality level and the emerging transfemicide-crime trend under which the region sits.

records.name: Durango
records.current_summary:
No Durango-specific laws, incidents or enforcement patterns are supported by the vetted sources for this map. The national picture governs: by March 2025 an international human-rights organization counted 22 of Mexico's 32 states as having legislated legal gender-recognition procedures, with six state legislatures enacting none; a March 2024 report from the same organization documents that where no procedure exists, trans people face police stops, denied documents and institutional mistreatment.

Transfeminicide has become a criminal category in some states — the capital imposes up to 70 years — against more than 95% homicide impunity nationally, and reporting finds convictions lag the statutes. For a visitor, Durango's own documented record is thin: expect the country-wide picture, neither verified local protections nor verified local hostility.
